signals.title: @arnaudmercier: Espionnage en orbite et pouvoir de l’information : https://t.co/fYMh40Ijgt "Traduction en français : Résumé Les satellites de reconnaissance
signals.content: Espionnage en orbite et pouvoir de l’information : https://t.co/fYMh40Ijgt "Traduction en français : Résumé Les satellites de reconnaissance permettent d’observer l’état des installations militaires d’un État cible sans pénétrer dans son espace aérien souverain. Les informations ainsi obtenues peuvent influencer des opérations militaires menées à plusieurs milliers de kilomètres de distance. Toutefois, l’observation d’un territoire, l’intervention dans des systèmes bénéficiant d’une protection juridique, le soutien apporté aux parties à un conflit et l’emploi de la force constituent des actes distincts, assortis de conséquences juridiques différentes. Il n’existe donc pas de règle unique de droit international susceptible de résoudre de manière uniforme l’ensemble de ces questions. Le présent article examine dans quelles circonstances les informations recueillies en orbite cessent d’être une simple source d’avantage stratégique pour devenir un acte juridiquement significatif. À travers une analyse dogmatique du droit de l’espace, de la Charte des Nations Unies, du droit de la responsabilité internationale des États et du droit international humanitaire, l’étude développe le cadre conceptuel de la « conversion juridique de l’information ». Ce cadre examine les situations dans lesquelles l’acquisition, la diffusion ou l’utilisation opérationnelle de données satellitaires se rattache à des obligations spécifiques de droit international. En s’appuyant sur des sources publiques relatives aux programmes de satellites de reconnaissance de la péninsule coréenne, au système satellitaire israélien Ofek 19 et aux images satellitaires fournies commercialement à l’Ukraine, l’article met en lumière à la fois l’importance militaire de l’observation depuis l’orbite et les limites inhérentes à tout raisonnement juridique fondé sur des informations ouvertes. L’article rejette l’assimilation immédiate d’une observation étrangère à une attaque armée, tout en récusant l’idée selon laquelle la liberté des activités dans l’espace extra-atmosphérique exonérerait automatiquement toute utilisation ultérieure de l’information de toute responsabilité juridique. Il propose une approche juridique fondée sur les circonstances factuelles concrètes, de nature à protéger les intérêts de sécurité des États souverains, à préserver les conditions juridiques du recours à la force en légitime défense et à prendre en compte les effets sur les populations civiles dépendantes de services spatiaux communs." "偵察衛星は、対象国の領空に侵入することなく軍事施設の状況を把握することができ、そこから得られた情報は、数千キロメートル離れた場所で実施される軍事作戦に影響を与える可能性がある。しかし、領域の観測、法的保護の対象となるシステムへの介入、交戦当事者への支援、および武力の行使は、それぞれ異なる法的帰結を伴う行為であるため、これらをめぐる問題を一律に解決する単一の国際法規則は存在しない。本論文は、軌道上で収集された情報が、単なる戦略的優位性の源泉を超えて、いかなる状況において法的に重要な行為となるのかを検討するものである。 本研究では、宇宙法、国際連合憲章、国家責任法および国際人道法に関する法教義学的分析を通じて、「情報の法的転換」という概念的枠組みを展開する。これは、衛星データの取得、流通または作戦上の利用が、特定可能な国際法上の義務と結び付く状況を検討するものである。朝鮮半島における偵察衛星計画、イスラエルのOfek 19衛星システム、およびウクライナに商業的に提供された衛星画像に関する公開資料を用い、軌道上からの観測が有する軍事的重要性と、公開情報に基づいて法的推論を行う際の限界の双方を明らかにする。 本論文は、外国による観測行為を直ちに武力攻撃と同一視する考え方を退ける一方、宇宙空間における活動の自由によって、その後の情報利用がすべて法的責任から免除されるという見解も否定する。そして、主権国家の安全保障上の利益を保護しつつ、自衛のための武力行使に関する法的要件を維持し、さらに共通の宇宙サービスに依存する民間人への影響にも配慮する、具体的事実関係に即した法的対応のあり方を提示する。" "1 Orbital Espionage and the Power of Information State Sovereignty, Military Intelligence and the Limits of Self-Defence under International Law Silvio Moreira Alves Júnior Brazilian Attorney - Independent Researcher silviojr.adv@outlook.com https://t.co/08Urt6Tvur 2026 Abstract Orbital reconnaissance has intensified legal questions surrounding the observation of strategic assets, the circulation of satellite-derived information and its use in military decision-making. This article examines the relationship between space-based intelligence, State sovereignty and the legal frameworks applicable to international conduct. The central research question concerns the circumstances in which the collection, transfer or operational employment of orbital information requires legal assessment under international law. The study adopts a qualitative, doctrinal and documentary approach based on the Outer Space Treaty, the Charter of the United Nations, the law of State responsibility and relevant rules of international humanitarian law. Publicly available material concerning Korean reconnaissance programmes, Israel’s Ofek 19 satellite and commercial satellite imagery provided in connection with the conflict in Ukraine is considered as documentary context. The Theory of Dynamic Adaptive Warfare is used to situate the strategic role of information while keeping the doctrinal legal analysis analytically distinct. The discussion addresses the jurisdictional framework for orbital observation, the participation of public and private actors, the scope and limits of the documentary record, and the legal standards relevant to possible State responses. 2 Keywords: Orbital Espionage. State Sovereignty. Military Intelligence. Law. War. Space. International Space Law. Self-defence. 1. Introduction: The State That Can Be Seen but Cannot Exclude the Observer Sovereignty traditionally gives a State authority over its territory and the airspace above it, yet orbital observation has made a portion of its most sensitive security environment visible to foreign governments without a conventional border crossing. A military base can remain inaccessible to outsiders on the ground while its construction, patterns of movement and apparent operational readiness become the subject of repeated satellite collection. The contradiction is not that sovereignty has disappeared or that outer space belongs to whoever possesses the strongest satellites. It is that the ability to obtain consequential knowledge has become partly separated from the territorial power to prevent physical entry, creating a legal dispute that begins with information but can end with coercion. Treating the subject only as espionage would miss the character of this separation; treating it only as space law would miss the consequences of turning an image into a military decision. The central research question is therefore narrower and more difficult than whether reconnaissance satellites are generally lawful: under what conditions can the acquisition or use of information collected from orbit constitute an internationally relevant wrong, and what remedies remain available to the State whose security is exposed? The proposed answer is that strategic sensitivity is not itself a source of international prohibition. Legal relevance emerges when a particular method of collection, intervention in another State's protected interests, attributable assistance to unlawful conduct or operation in an armed conflict satisfies the elements of an applicable rule. This distinction is consequential because a State may know with confidence that it is being watched while lacking evidence of a specific breach, and the temptation to close that 3 evidentiary gap with the language of self-defence risks converting insecurity into an asserted entitlement to force. The analysis is doctrinal and documentary rather than quantitative. It interprets the Outer Space Treaty alongside the Charter of the United Nations, the International Law Commission's rules on State responsibility and the law of armed conflict, then compares that framework with limited but verifiable public records of contemporary reconnaissance systems. The article draws on the Theory of Dynamic Adaptive Warfare (TDAW) to explain why information changes military choice, and on earlier work on orbital sovereignty to identify the jurisdictional setting, without reproducing a theory of orbital escalation or attempting to measure the probability of conflict (Alves Júnior, 2026a, 2026b). Its distinct contribution is a juridical account of informational advantage: knowledge may alter a State's vulnerability profoundly while the grounds for responsibility and the lawful range of responses remain questions to be established separately. 2. The Jurisdictional Paradox of Remote Observation Article 1 of the Chicago Convention establishes complete and exclusive sovereignty in the airspace above national territory, but the law applicable to outer space does not simply extend this territorial model upward indefinitely. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 protects freedom of exploration and use in Article I, excludes national appropriation through sovereign claims in Article II and requires conformity with international law, including the United Nations Charter, in Article III (International Civil Aviation Organization, 1944; United Nations, 1967). Neither instrument establishes an agreed numerical boundary between airspace and outer space, which means that analysis should not quietly assume a fixed internationally accepted altitude. For activities conducted in what States consistently treat as orbital space, however, it would be misleading to describe each passage over foreign territory as the equivalent of an unauthorised 4 reconnaissance aircraft entering sovereign airspace. The observer does not acquire territorial authority by orbiting, but the observed State does not acquire an automatic territorial veto over the orbit. This allocation of freedoms leaves a politically uncomfortable but legally important result. The target of observation may have legitimate national-security interests, and those interests may be put at risk by the accumulation of images that disclose patterns no single photograph would reveal. Yet injury to secrecy is not identical to a violation of sovereignty, because international law does not establish a comprehensive right to exclude all observation of territory from space. The principle of non-intervention requires attention to coercive interference in matters reserved to a State, not merely to the existence of foreign interest in those matters. Satellite reconnaissance may support later unlawful interference, but a legal conclusion about that later interference cannot be projected backwards onto the orbit as if the collection itself necessarily contained every element of the subsequent offence. The 1986 Principles Relating to Remote Sensing of the Earth from Outer Space require a careful qualification. Their definition of remote sensing is tied to improving natural-resource management, land use and environmental protection, so they cannot simply be transposed to classified military reconnaissance. Within that defined field, the principles address respect for sensed States, cooperation and access to primary and processed data on non-discriminatory and reasonable-cost terms (United Nations General Assembly, 1986, principles I and XII). They are General Assembly principles rather than a treaty conferring a general veto over satellite observation, and they do not establish an unconditional right to obtain classified military imagery. Their relevance to the present inquiry is therefore contextual rather than determinative: they demonstrate the international concern for the interests of observed States while leaving any 5 allegation concerning military intelligence to be examined under the law actually applicable to that conduct. The relevance of sovereignty is clearest when a dispute is framed as a demand to control the intelligence product rather than a demand to control the orbit. Information about a military installation may be sensitive, expensive to conceal and capable of informing coercive diplomacy, yet international law has not established an exclusive property right held by the territorial State over every representation of its territory produced from outside its jurisdiction. A claim founded only on the State's preference for secrecy therefore differs from a claim founded on unlawful entry, a binding confidentiality obligation or harmful interference with a protected system. That distinction need not disable diplomacy or domestic regulation. States may protect military sites against unauthorised access, regulate classified disclosures within their jurisdiction and employ counterintelligence, but they cannot infer from those domestic authorities an extraterritorial power to prohibit all observation from outer space. Defining the legal interest accurately makes both claims and restraint more credible, because it leaves room for a right to object to genuinely unlawful conduct without constructing a sovereignty rule that treaty practice does not support. That distinction also clarifies the role of Article IX of the Outer Space Treaty, which calls for due regard to corresponding interests and provides for consultations concerning activities that may cause potentially harmful interference. Due regard is not a general authorisation for a sensed State to forbid all strategically unwelcome information-gathering, but neither is freedom of use a licence to disregard harm, dangerous proximity operations or interference with other space systems. A satellite that observes passively and one that intentionally disrupts a spacecraft's communications may occupy the same orbital environment while presenting legally different questions. The 6 operative facts are the conduct, effects, applicable obligations and evidence of any interference, not the adjective 'military' attached to the mission. 3. Information as an Object of Power, Not an Automatic International Wrong Intelligence is valuable because it reshapes the choices available to institutions that can use it. Persistent observation can reduce uncertainty about deployment, reveal a departure from ordinary activity, corroborate information from human sources or expose deception. The reduction of uncertainty is not equivalent to certainty about intent: a photograph can document the presence of an object without establishing why it is present, whether the activity is lawful or what a commander intends to do next. This difference becomes even more important when remote-sensing products are combined with communications interception, public sources and algorithmic analysis. A sophisticated intelligence picture may be strategically persuasive yet incapable, by itself, of proving the legal elements of a prohibited act. The concept of informational power developed here is relational rather than proprietary. The State collecting data gains potential influence over its own decisions and sometimes over an ally's conduct, while the State observed loses a measure of practical secrecy without necessarily losing any jurisdiction recognised by international law. These consequences should not be confused. Intelligence about missile movements could serve strategic warning, verification, targeting or diplomatic de-escalation, and the legal assessment changes when the information is used in a course of conduct that international law regulates. An image does not carry a fixed legal character through every subsequent transaction. The same dataset can be lawfully collected, contractually transferred, misinterpreted, relied upon in an unlawful attack or used to prevent an attack on civilians; determining its significance requires examining identifiable actions and actors rather than assigning liability to 'information' as an abstraction. 7 A different risk arises when analysts and officials move from a claim of strategic harm to a claim of legal injury without identifying the obligation said to have been broken. The possibility that foreign intelligence will be used against national security is real, but the fact of that possibility cannot eliminate the difference between evidence of observation and evidence of prohibited coercion. Nor should this analysis imply that all intelligence methods are immune from challenge. Intrusion into sovereign airspace, harmful interference with satellites, violations of specific international commitments and military operations prohibited by the law of force may be unlawful even when motivated by intelligence collection. The article's point is not to protect espionage as a legal category; it is to avoid using that contested label in place of the legal elements that must actually be demonstrated. This account gives the TDAW an appropriately limited function. The theory explains war as an adaptive environment in which information and human judgement condition action across domains, but the legal argument in this article does not depend on proving a forecast of escalation or importing a full theory of conflict into every doctrinal issue (Alves Júnior, 2026b). The informational advantage generated in orbit becomes relevant to law only through conduct, institutional responsibility and a rule applicable to that conduct. The strategic significance of the information thus explains why the problem matters, while legal analysis determines which consequences can be justified, challenged or remedied. 4. Who Acts When the Satellite Is Commercial? Commercial providers complicate legal characterisation because the owner of a spacecraft, the State of registry, the government that licenses operations, the purchaser of imagery and the armed force that eventually uses the product may be different actors. The Outer Space Treaty makes States internationally responsible for national activities in outer space, including those of 8 non-governmental entities, and requires authorisation and continuing supervision under Article VI. Article VIII preserves jurisdiction and control over registered space objects and their personnel in the relevant terms, but jurisdiction over an object should not be mistaken for sovereignty over the Earth territory beneath its orbit. The treaty system therefore creates regulatory responsibilities without collapsing all downstream intelligence transactions into one State act (United Nations, 1967). Responsibility under Article VI also needs to be distinguished from attribution under the general law of State responsibility. The International Law Commission's Articles on Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts identify circumstances in which conduct of State organs, entities exercising governmental authority and persons acting on State instructions or under its direction or control can be attributed to a State. Licensing a commercial satellite is not, without more, proof that every delivery of imagery to every customer constitutes the licensing State's own internationally wrongful operation (International Law Commission, 2001). Equally, the commercial form of an activity does not make it immune from accountability where evidence establishes direction, control, adoption or another relevant basis of attribution. The institutional and contractual facts matter as much as the satellite's orbit. A possible allegation of aid or assistance requires similar care. Under Article 16 of the International Law Commission's Articles, responsibility for aid or assistance concerns an internationally wrongful act of another State, the assisting State's knowledge of the circumstances and conduct that would be wrongful if committed by the assisting State itself, subject to the rule's further conditions and its commentary (International Law Commission, 2001). That provision addresses responsibility between States; a private company's supply contract does not, without a legally sufficient connection to a State, satisfy its attribution requirements. Evidence that a 9 company supplied imagery to a defence ministry does not by itself establish the principal wrongful act or the elements of State aid or assistance. Equally, contractual opacity is not conclusive evidence of innocence. Military usefulness, legal attribution and possible complicity remain analytically independent propositions, and each must survive scrutiny on its own facts. This is particularly necessary where information assists a State in exercising a lawful right of defence, because the existence of armed conflict does not render every act supporting one participant wrongful. The inquiry becomes more exacting when intelligence is supplied to an armed force during an international armed conflict. A commercial product can shorten targeting timelines and contribute directly to a particular operation, but it does not follow that every image purchased by a belligerent makes the supplier a combatant or that each State connected to the transaction becomes a party to the conflict. The legal assessment must examine the nature of the assistance, the supplier's conduct and the factual and legal basis for any asserted responsibility, including the circumstances of a concrete attack. For parties bound by Additional Protocol I, Article 52(2) defines military objectives by reference to an object's nature, location, purpose or use, its effective contribution to military action and the definite military advantage offered by its destruction, capture or neutralisation; the core distinction is also reflected in customary humanitarian law. Qualification cannot rest simply on the nationality of the owner or the political identity of a customer (Additional Protocol I, 1977, art. 52(2)). This disaggregation is particularly important for satellites that support both civilian and military services. Navigation, communications and imaging infrastructure can assist armed forces and sustain hospitals, emergency response, agriculture and civilian transport at the same time. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has highlighted the humanitarian consequences 10 of disrupting space services on which essential civilian functions depend (ICRC, 2024). A State contemplating action against such infrastructure must therefore consider the actual military use and the expected civilian effects rather than treating commercial status as absolute protection or military use as blanket permission to attack. The capacity of space technology to serve several purposes makes the factual assessment harder; it does not remove distinction, proportionality and precautions when the law of armed conflict applies. 5. The Contemporary Record: Three Different Forms of Dependence on Orbital Knowledge Recent public announcements illustrate three distinct relationships between orbital observation and State security, although they cannot disclose the classified collection plans or operational decisions that would be necessary for a definitive legal assessment. On the Korean Peninsula, the Republic of Korea reported the completion of its military reconnaissance satellite 425 Project in November 2025, describing improved day-and-night monitoring of North Korean activity (Republic of Korea Ministry of National Defense, 2025). The launch of reconnaissance spacecraft by the Democratic People's Republic of Korea has also been addressed within a separate Security Council framework concerning prohibited ballistic-missile-related activities (United Nations Security Council, 2023). These facts should not be flattened into a claim that collecting an image is unlawful for one side and lawful for the other by reason of political alignment. A restriction concerning a particular launch technology and an allegation concerning the later acquisition of information are legally separate questions. Their coexistence demonstrates why the juridical object of a complaint must be identified with precision. Israel's Ofek 19 offers a different illustration. In September 2025 the Israeli Ministry of Defense stated that the satellite's radar system had returned its first high-resolution images following launch, identifying its role in geospatial intelligence (Israel Ministry of Defense, 2025). 11 The announcement provides credible evidence of a reconnaissance capability and a declared defence purpose. It does not reveal which foreign military facilities were imaged, how the data entered operational planning, whether a particular strike relied on it or whether the relevant legal obligations were respected in any subsequent action. Drawing a stronger conclusion from the available statement would manufacture certainty that the evidence does not support. The example is useful precisely because it..."

signals.title: Rovoxia/AI-Phone-Debloater
signals.content: An Open-Source Universal rootless Android ADB debloater & bloatware remover. 100% fail-safe with auto-snapshots, zero data loss & 320+ OEM rules (Samsung One UI, Xiaomi HyperOS, Pixel, OnePlus/BBK, Moto, Tecno). Built for CLI & AI agents (Claude Code, ChatGPT, Gemini).
signals.score_reason: high-value open-source ecosystem signal; agentic AI relevance. Final score: 70. Freshness: source age 0d.
signals.brief_en:
Title: Rovoxia/AI-Phone-Debloater

An open‑source, universal, root‑less Android ADB debloater and bloatware remover. It operates without requiring device rooting, using ADB commands to uninstall or disable system apps. The tool includes automatic snapshots before each change, guaranteeing a fail‑safe rollback and zero data loss. It incorporates more than 320 OEM‑specific rules covering Samsung One UI, Xiaomi HyperOS, Google Pixel, OnePlus/BBK, Motorola, Tecno and others, ensuring compatibility across major manufacturers. Designed for command‑line use and integration with AI agents (Claude Code, ChatGPT, Gemini), it enables automated, strategic device hygiene while preserving user data. Claims are based on publicly available source code and documentation; real‑world performance may vary depending on device state and OEM updates.

أداة مفتوحة المصدر لإزالة التطبيقات المزعجة (bloatware) من أجهزة أندرويد عبر ADB دون الحاجة إلى روت. تعمل بدون روت باستخدام أوامر ADB لإلغاء تثبيت أو تعطيل التطبيقات النظامية. تتضمن لقطات احتياطية تلقائية قبل كل تعديل، ما يضمن إمكانية الرجوع إلى الحالة السابقة دون فقدان البيانات. تحتوي على أكثر من 320 قاعدة مخصصة لمصنّعي الأجهزة مثل سامسونج One UI، شاومي HyperOS، جوجل بيكسل، ون بلس/BBK، موتورولا، تيكنو وغيرها، لضمان التوافق عبر معظم العلامات التجارية. صُممت للاستخدام عبر سطر الأوامر وتكامل مع وكلاء الذكاء الاصطناعي (Claude Code، ChatGPT، Gemini)، مما يتيح أتمتة صيانة الأجهزة بشكل استراتيجي مع الحفاظ على البيانات. المعلومات مستندة إلى الكود المصدري والوثائق العامة؛ قد تختلف النتائج الفعلية حسب حالة الجهاز وتحديثات الشركات المصنعة.

العنوان: michaelalber/ai-toolkit

نظرة عامة: مستودع جاهز للإنتاج يقدم أدوات وبرامج وكيل مدعومة بالذكاء الاصطناعي متوافقة مع Claude Code و OpenCode و Pi. يتضمن أمثلة وقوالب لتطوير مدفوع بالاختبار (TDD) عبر .NET وPython وRust، بالإضافة إلى نماذج نشر الذكاء الاصطناعي على الحافة. المحتوى مفتوح المصدر ويظهر أنه يُحدَّث بانتظام، إلا أن مدى الاعتماد الفعلي في بيئات الإنتاج ونتائج الأداء لا تزال غير موثقة.

نقاط رئيسية:
- دعم متعدد اللغات: .NET، Python، Rust.
- تركيز على توليد الكود الآلي باستخدام الذكاء الاصطناعي.
- يتضمن سير عمل TDD وإرشادات دمج الذكاء الاصطناعي على الحافة.
- مستودع عام؛ النشاط يشير إلى تحديثات حديثة، لكن مؤشرات الأثر محدودة.

الآثار: قد يسرّع تطوير النماذج الأولية للفرق التي تستخدم مساعدين برمجيين مدعومين بالذكاء الاصطناعي، خاصةً في بيئات تقنية متنوعة. يُنصح بالتحقق من الصلاحية في بيئات الإنتاج قبل الاعتماد على نطاق واسع.

signals.brief_en: AnhDuongVo/ai-scientist introduces an agentic workflow for literature-informed protein binder design. The system orchestrates NVIDIA BioNeMo NIMs (RFdiffusion, ProteinMPNN, and Boltz-2) to generate ranked candidate reports with literature citations. Operates on a local simulator by default, with a single flag configuration enabling real-world NIM integration.

signals.title: @grok: Brutally honest: AI already outperforms physicians on pure diagnostic accuracy in controlled complex cases (Microsoft MAI-DxO ~2x better). B
signals.content: Brutally honest: AI already outperforms physicians on pure diagnostic accuracy in controlled complex cases (Microsoft MAI-DxO ~2x better). By ~2030 it will likely beat humans on core cognitive work like diagnosis, test selection, and chronic management. It still cannot examine, biopsy, operate, or fully own liability and the human relationship. Full job replacement is not happening in the next 10-15 years—and maybe never without advanced robotics plus regulatory and patient acceptance. Expect heavy augmentation instead.
